newsitem.title: UK: STERLING EXTENDS SLIDE, FRESH LOSSES SEEN.
newsitem.headline: STERLING EXTENDS SLIDE, FRESH LOSSES SEEN.

text.p: Sterling's free-fall accelerated on Friday as it tumbled over five pfennigs and 2.5 cents to below 2.93 marks and $1.57 but analyst say the ride is not over - despite a drop of over four percent this week.
"The pace of the fall has been amazing....But there is still scope on the downside and we could possibly go back to 2.90-marks," said Audrey Childe-Freeman, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
But analysts said a short breather at current levels was now in order before the battered unit headed south again.
"I see a bottom around here, for the time being...But we have an end-year target of 2.80 marks," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN AMRO.
At 1115 GMT, sterling/mark was trading at 2.9305/15 against 2.9690/00 in late Europe on Thursday, and well off peaks of 2.9825 hit earlier on Friday.
Cable was at $1.5708/18 against $1.5880/90 in late Europe on Thursday and well down from peaks of $1.5940 hit early.
The bloodied unit has tumbled nearly 14 pfennigs and nearly seven cents this week from highs of 3.0633 marks and $1.6345, it's sharpest weekly fall so far this year.

Sterling, on a losing streak since Wednesday, crumbled after the Bank of England hiked base rates by a 1/4 of a point to 7.0 percent on Thursday and signalled that rates had reached levels consistent with inflation targets.

Traders said the Bank knocked the wind out of sterling as it seemed to indicate a lid to further rate rises, prompting profit-taking and liquidation from UK clearers and U.S. funds on Friday, said traders. A buoyant mark against the dollar on Friday also weighed on the British unit.
"The sterling bubble has well and truly burst," said ABN Amro's Norfield.

Sterling rocketed from lows of 2.2747 marks in August 1996 to multi-year peaks of 3.0878 marks in late July as the market banked on higher rates to cool a robust economy and investors piled into sterling as a safe haven from the possibility of a soft euro.

"I think sterling would now need a shock to get back above 3.0 marks. But to get above 3.0 marks it would need a major turnaround in UK data," said Mike Metcalfe, treasury economist at NatWest Markets.
Metcalfe, however, said the pound was likely to pause for a breather at current levels before attempting a fresh slide.
"It's a brave thing to speculate...How soon sterling is going to find its floor is going to depend on UK data next week," he added.
"It is going to find a bottom," he said, adding that maybe 2.90 marks would be it.
